fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Two nativities that cannot be reconciled", "body": "John McHugh traces his whole research life to a seventh grade classroom, where Sister Virginia Consolata had the class read Matthew and Luke back to back. The students looked up realizing the two birth accounts contradict each other. Matthew has a star, Babylonian astrologers, a house and only Mary. Luke has a census, a caravanserai courtyard, a manger, shepherds and a heavenly army, and never mentions a star at all. McHugh notes that nobody at Jesus's adult ministry had attended his birth, so neither evangelist had eyewitness testimony to work from."}, {"title": "Reading the sky as a written text", "body": "The core claim McHugh brings to Chance Garton is that Babylonian astrologers called the night sky Shittir Shammay, heavenly writing, and called an astrologer a tupsharu, meaning author or writer. Constellations were still frames of history, and the cuneiform spellings of their titles carried secondary meanings that supplied the action and the details. Esarhaddon, a seventh century Assyrian king, boasted on a monolith that he wrote his name in Lumashi writing, constellation writing, which McHugh jokes was the ancient equivalent of giving away the trade secret on Twitter."}, {"title": "The virgin, the child king and the manger", "body": "The tableau McHugh builds sits in one stretch of sky. Virgo is parthenos, the virgin, in Greek atlases, while her western stars form a Mesopotamian pregnancy goddess named Eru. Regulus in Leo is Sheru, a homonym meaning both king and child, giving an infant king. Just west sits M44 in Cancer, the star cluster the Greeks called the manger. Read together with Absin, whose readings yield maratu, both bitter and sea, you get Miriam or bitter sea. Mary, the child king and the feeding trough are all in one view."}, {"title": "Where Luke found his shepherds and angels", "body": "McHugh argues Luke pulled his cast from the constellations flanking that tableau. Orion, low in the west, is titled sepa or reu, shepherd or shepherds, and also suka, a deified messenger, which is angel of the Lord. Libra rising in the southeast is written dingir gish erin, and erin also renders sabu, army, producing army of heaven. Leo's poetic title labu doubles as the verb to wrap up, Lugal doubles as a fine cloth, and M44 is fatne, manger, spelling out a firstborn son swaddled and laid in a manger."}, {"title": "Miracles, paganism and December 25th", "body": "Because the ancients read the sky as literal history, McHugh says miracles were genuinely possible to them. Orion steps onto the celestial waters seven centuries before Jesus, and his cuneiform titles include Dingir Damu, son god, and Sukal, anointed one. Chance Garton and McHugh push the idea outward to Moses, the golden fleece, Pegasus and even the seven kings of Rome. McHugh closes on the solstice, when the sun stands still for several days and then turns north again, sol invictus, which is why Jesus was assigned a December 25th birthday."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: John McHugh is a scholar of Middle-East & Native American archeo-astronomy, who has found an incredible linguistic explanation for mythological miracle stories. These scriptural pseudo-histories have long been believed to be founded in real events of the distant past, yet with McHugh's examination of the Sumerian/Akkadian cuneiform languages and star-atlases, the stellar origins of theological teachings may have been discovered at last.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Check out the new InnerVerse merch store and support the show with original art creations!
